source_note: arXiv record and Science DOI verify publication in 2022.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Combines large-scale code generation with filtering and clustering to solve competitive programming problems.
key_findings: The reported system reaches a competitive level on held-out contests by searching over many candidate programs.
importance: It demonstrates the interaction of generation scale, execution filters and selection in achieving code-task performance.
relevance: The manuscript's conclusions about persistence require compute-matched baselines: extra attempts can help when selection is informative.
transferable_idea: Compare sequential revision with independent candidate search under the same token and execution budget, using a separately validated selector.
limitations: Competitive-programming performance is not security repair, and large candidate budgets can hide weak individual-sample reliability or imperfect filtering.

title: Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models
authors: Andy K. Zhang; Neil Perry; Riya Dulepet; Joey Ji; Celeste Menders; Justin W. Lin; Eliot Jones; Gashon Hussein; Samantha Liu; Donovan Jasper; Pura Peetathawatchai; Ari Glenn; Vikram Sivashankar; Daniel Zamoshchin; Leo Glikbarg; Derek Askaryar; Mike Yang; Teddy Zhang; Rishi Alluri; Nathan Tran; Rinnara Sangpisit; Polycarpos Yiorkadjis; Kenny Osele; Gautham Raghupathi; Dan Boneh; Daniel E. Ho; Percy Liang
source_note: arXiv author record identifies ICLR 2025.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Provides a reproducible benchmark of cybersecurity capture-the-flag challenges with executable environments and intermediate subgoals.
key_findings: The evaluated agents show substantial limitations, while subtask scaffolding helps expose which stages prevent completion.
importance: It offers a bridge from small synthetic security tasks to richer executable security environments.
relevance: The manuscript should test whether its feedback mechanism persists when agents must discover files, tools and exploit conditions.
transferable_idea: Select a small number of auditable tasks with independent replayable security outcomes and annotate progress before and after feedback interventions.
limitations: Offensive challenge completion is different from secure repair; CTF flags and challenge design do not certify defense quality or real-world deployment safety.

title: CyberGym: Evaluating AI Agents' Real-World Cybersecurity Capabilities at Scale
authors: Zhun Wang; Tianneng Shi; Jingxuan He; Matthew Cai; Jialin Zhang; Dawn Song
source_note: ICLR 2026 primary OpenReview PDF verified; use current published title rather than older preprint title.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Builds a large executable cybersecurity benchmark from real vulnerable software and evaluates agents on producing vulnerability-revealing inputs.
key_findings: The study reports successful reproduction on some real targets and discovery of additional defects during evaluation.
importance: It supplies concrete security outcomes linked to actual software, beyond source-token heuristics.
relevance: The manuscript's strongest external validity test would pair proposed patches with independently replayed attack inputs and benign functionality checks.
transferable_idea: Use reproducible proof-of-concept inputs to measure whether a misleading verdict causes a previously blocked attack to become effective again.
limitations: Attack reproduction and patch completeness are different objectives; absence of a reproduced exploit does not prove that a patch is secure.

title: AppWorld: A Controllable World of Apps and People for Benchmarking Interactive Coding Agents
authors: Harsh Trivedi; Tushar Khot; Mareike Hartmann; Ruskin Manku; Vinty Dong; Edward Li; Shashank Gupta; Ashish Sabharwal; Niranjan Balasubramanian
source_note: ACL 2024 proceedings verified; arXiv describes camera-ready version.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Creates a controllable ecosystem of simulated applications, users and APIs for evaluating interactive coding agents.
key_findings: Tasks are evaluated through state changes and collateral effects; the benchmark reveals difficulty even for strong agents.
importance: It treats satisfying the request and preserving unrelated desirable state as joint requirements.
relevance: The manuscript's overblocking cases likewise show that denying every request can appear secure while violating the legitimate task.
transferable_idea: Represent security and utility as separate invariants, then require both across the trajectory rather than only at the final verdict.
limitations: Simulated app tasks and authored assertions remain bounded specifications; their completeness must be audited before transferring conclusions.

title: AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use
authors: Junzhi Chen; Harsh Trivedi; Jane Pan; Michael JQ Zhang; Tejas Srinivasan; Niranjan Balasubramanian; Ashish Sabharwal
source_note: ICML 2026 PMLR volume 306, pages 16996–17023, independently confirms venue beyond the arXiv author comment.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Extends AppWorld with tasks requiring clarification, confirmation and communication about infeasible instructions.
key_findings: The 516-task benchmark reports that correct user interaction is essential and that compositional scenarios remain particularly difficult.
importance: It expands the decision space beyond acting versus stopping to include resolving ambiguity with a user.
relevance: The manuscript's stopping problem may sometimes be an evidence-acquisition or clarification problem rather than a binary abstention decision.
transferable_idea: Offer an explicit checker-disagreement escalation action and evaluate whether it preserves security without excessive deferral.
limitations: The user is simulated with specified knowledge boundaries; interaction quality and feasibility in real developer workflows require separate validation.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
authors: Edoardo Debenedetti; Jie Zhang; Mislav Balunović; Luca Beurer-Kellner; Marc Fischer; Florian Tramèr
source_note: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks primary proceedings verified.
access_depth: Primary abstract and bibliographic record; results not independently reproduced
contribution: Provides a dynamic benchmark for tool-use agents exposed to prompt injections in untrusted data.
key_findings: The study evaluates both ordinary task utility and resilience to attacks, exposing tradeoffs across defenses and models.
importance: It makes the trust boundary between instructions and environmental content explicit.
relevance: The manuscript's misleading checker output can be studied as an environmental reliability problem while remaining distinct from malicious prompt injection.
transferable_idea: Label evidence sources and authority, compare accidental and adversarial verdict corruption, and score security together with legitimate task completion.
limitations: Injection defenses do not automatically protect against a semantically wrong but correctly formatted trusted checker; that distinction needs experimental isolation.

title: PatchBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Vulnerability Patching
authors: Chihao Shen; Jiacheng Li; Aastha Mahajan; Jeffery Siyuan Tian; Yonghwi Kwon; Yizheng Chen
access_depth: full text: introduction, benchmark construction, validation, results
contribution: Builds a vulnerability-repair benchmark that tests root-cause repair, contamination, and preservation of intended behavior.
key_findings: Across eleven agents, PoC-only validation inflates reported solve rates by 1.83 times on average.
importance: A direct modern challenge to treating exploit suppression as repair.
relevance: The manuscript's weak-check disagreements and reject-all outcomes belong to an established validation problem.
transferable_idea: Reuse separate malicious and benign input corpora; intervene on feedback only after independently validating a candidate.
limitations: Reference-patch behavior and finite fuzzing remain imperfect; its aggregate rates are not baselines for the local finite tasks.

title: Patch Validation in Automated Vulnerability Repair
authors: Zheng Yu; Wenxuan Shi; Xinqian Sun; Zheyun Feng; Meng Xu; Xinyu Xing
access_depth: full text: methods, validation results, manual assessment
contribution: Introduces PVBench and developer-derived PoC+ tests that encode post-fix semantics.
key_findings: In 209 cases across twenty projects, 42.3% of patches passing basic validation fail PoC+ tests across the evaluated configurations.
importance: Shows that even exploit plus existing functional tests can miss intended behavior.
relevance: Precludes novelty claims based solely on adding a stronger second checker.
transferable_idea: Include developer-intent tests and adjudicate remaining semantic disagreements; keep oracle specificity explicit.
limitations: Some PoC+ passes still circumvent checks; developer equivalence is a demanding criterion, not a universal security proof.

title: Vul4Py: Benchmarking Automated Vulnerability Repair in Python with Paired Exploit and Functional Oracles
authors: Tan Bui; Ting Zhang; Ferdian Thung; Yunpeng Xiong; Penghao Jiang; Xin Zhou; David Lo
access_depth: primary abstract and metadata
contribution: Packages one hundred real Python vulnerabilities with exploit and project-native functional checks.
key_findings: The paired oracle rejects fifteen of 119 patches accepted by exploit-only checking.
importance: Offers a directly relevant executable Python benchmark with functionality preservation built into acceptance.
relevance: The manuscript's finite CSRF overblocking should be distinguished from genuinely unsafe acceptance using this two-dimensional logic.
transferable_idea: Adapt selected real-project tasks into matched feedback forks, keeping independent exploit and legitimate-use results.
limitations: Results concern its selected vulnerabilities and tools; neither paired tests nor manual equivalence certify all security properties.

title: Improving LLM-Assisted Secure Code Generation through Retrieval-Augmented-Generation and Multi-Tool Feedback
authors: Vidyut Sriram; Sawan Pandita; Achintya Lakshmanan; Aneesh Shamraj; Suman Saha
access_depth: primary abstract and metadata
contribution: Combines retrieved successful repairs with compiler, CodeQL, and symbolic-execution feedback.
key_findings: Reports improved measured security outcomes for DeepSeek-Coder and CodeLlama on its generated-program dataset.
importance: Provides a concrete multi-tool repair pipeline against which feedback-source experiments can be positioned.
relevance: Unlike the historical fixed guidance condition, it performs semantic retrieval; the interventions must not share a RAG label.
transferable_idea: Vary agreement between heterogeneous tools while holding context length and information availability fixed.
limitations: Reported improvement is evaluator- and dataset-dependent; the abstract does not establish independent security completeness.

title: The Oracle Problem in Software Testing: A Survey
authors: Earl T. Barr; Mark Harman; Phil McMinn; Muzammil Shahbaz; Shin Yoo
access_depth: primary paper abstract; bibliographic metadata
contribution: Organizes approaches to deciding whether observed program behavior is correct.
key_findings: Distinguishes specification-based, derived, implicit, and human oracle information, with persistent automation limits.
importance: The foundational vocabulary makes clear that an evaluator is an assumption-bearing measurement instrument.
relevance: The manuscript currently treats several oracle roles together: property checks, policy acceptance, public feedback, and scientific adjudication.
transferable_idea: Define those roles separately and document provenance, scope, and failure modes for each.
limitations: A survey synthesizes prior work rather than supplying a new causal experiment; it cannot validate the local checker.

title: QuickCheck: A Lightweight Tool for Random Testing of Haskell Programs
authors: Koen Claessen; John Hughes
access_depth: primary abstract and conference metadata
contribution: Provides executable properties and customizable random generators for testing functional programs.
key_findings: Demonstrates lightweight generation of many test inputs from concise property descriptions.
importance: Established property-based testing as a practical alternative to a few hand-selected examples.
relevance: The manuscript's two-example checks are particularly vulnerable to untested boundaries and input combinations.
transferable_idea: Express preservation, rejection, and invariance properties, then generate legitimate and adversarial cases separately.
limitations: Random tests do not prove universal security; useful generators still require correct domain assumptions and assertions. Generator validity needs its own audit.

title: DART: Directed Automated Random Testing
authors: Patrice Godefroid; Nils Klarlund; Koushik Sen
access_depth: primary institutional abstract and metadata
contribution: Combines interface extraction, random test generation, and dynamic path-directed analysis.
key_findings: Automatically explores alternative execution paths without requiring manually written drivers for its supported programs.
importance: A foundational demonstration that test generation can systematically move beyond familiar examples.
relevance: Provides a stronger challenge-generation model than checking one SQL-injection payload or literal XSS string.
transferable_idea: Use path-directed input exploration in an executable-code extension and preserve discovered counterexamples.
limitations: Path exploration is constrained by environment models and solver support; coverage alone does not establish output correctness. Unsupported paths remain unresolved.

title: CUTE: A Concolic Unit Testing Engine for C
authors: Koushik Sen; Darko Marinov; Gul Agha
access_depth: primary institutional abstract and metadata
contribution: Extends combined concrete and symbolic execution to unit testing with pointer-rich memory graphs.
key_findings: Tracks constraints and incrementally constructs inputs that explore feasible execution paths.
importance: Shows how explicit program-state representations can produce targeted tests rather than superficial perturbations.
relevance: Relevant to moving the work from finite mode selection to realistic code whose behavior depends on structured inputs.
transferable_idea: Construct counterexample witnesses with explicit input-state requirements instead of merely returning FAIL.
limitations: The approach targets C and bounded exploration; adapting it to Python requires an appropriate execution and specification model.

title: KLEE: Unassisted and Automatic Generation of High-Coverage Tests for Complex Systems Programs
authors: Cristian Cadar; Daniel Dunbar; Dawson Engler
access_depth: full text: abstract, design overview, coverage results and limits
contribution: Develops scalable symbolic execution with environment modeling and constraint optimizations.
key_findings: Generates high coverage on real utilities and discovers previously unknown bugs.
importance: Demonstrates the feasibility of systematic executable validation beyond toy programs.
relevance: Useful for constructing stronger independent checks, while its own discussion separates coverage from semantic correctness.
transferable_idea: Use generated inputs and reference comparisons, logging which properties each check actually tests.
limitations: Environment models and path limits constrain conclusions; high coverage does not automatically provide a trustworthy semantic oracle. Unexplored paths must remain explicitly unknown.

title: Automated Whitebox Fuzz Testing
authors: Patrice Godefroid; Michael Y. Levin; David Molnar
access_depth: primary paper abstract/introduction and conference metadata
contribution: Uses symbolic constraints from concrete executions to generate new inputs for security testing.
key_findings: Demonstrates targeted exploration that can reach branches random mutation is unlikely to exercise.
importance: Connects security validation with systematic search over difficult input conditions.
relevance: The paper's weak fixtures cannot support broad safety claims without such adversarial challenge expansion.
transferable_idea: Compare feedback effects under weak tests versus stronger generated attack corpora, keeping evaluation hidden from the agent.
limitations: Fuzzing remains a bug-finding method, not a proof of absence; crashes are only one class of security outcome.

title: Finding and Understanding Bugs in C Compilers
authors: Xuejun Yang; Yang Chen; Eric Eide; John Regehr
access_depth: primary author abstract and metadata
contribution: Introduces Csmith, generating diverse C programs while avoiding undefined and unspecified behavior.
key_findings: The authors reported more than 325 previously unknown compiler bugs.
importance: Demonstrates that differential testing is useful only when the tested semantics are controlled.
relevance: Directly informs independent evaluator design: disagreement is uninterpretable when the task contract itself is ambiguous.
transferable_idea: Generate semantically valid task variants and compare independent implementations before exposing their verdicts to agents.
limitations: Agreement among implementations is not proof, and shared defects can survive differential checking. Preserve standards assumptions during comparison.

title: Compiler Validation via Equivalence Modulo Inputs
authors: Vu Le; Mehrdad Afshari; Zhendong Su
access_depth: primary paper abstract and introduction
contribution: Creates program variants equivalent on selected inputs to expose compiler inconsistencies.
key_findings: Its compiler-testing implementation uncovered numerous confirmed GCC and LLVM defects.
importance: Provides a precise example of conditional equivalence rather than claiming programs are globally interchangeable.
relevance: The manuscript's same-source matching is observational; controlled semantics-preserving transformations could test feedback robustness more cleanly.
transferable_idea: Create renaming and representation variants that preserve the bounded property, then test whether feedback responses survive them.
limitations: Equivalence holds for the defined inputs; transformation-induced task changes must be independently checked.

title: Automatically Finding Patches Using Genetic Programming
authors: Westley Weimer; ThanhVu Nguyen; Claire Le Goues; Stephanie Forrest
access_depth: primary paper abstract and metadata
contribution: Uses genetic programming and existing tests to evolve and minimize program repairs.
key_findings: Demonstrates automated repair without requiring a formal specification for each application.
importance: A foundational generate-and-validate architecture underlying later repair loops.
relevance: Shows why continuing after failure is ordinary search behavior; continuation alone is not evidence of irrationality.
transferable_idea: Include a simple non-LLM search baseline with the same acceptance signals and budgets.
limitations: Its tests encode an incomplete specification, and subsequent work challenges the correctness of many plausible repairs. Re-evaluation must therefore separate plausibility from correctness.

title: A Systematic Study of Automated Program Repair: Fixing 55 out of 105 Bugs for $8 Each
authors: Claire Le Goues; Michael Dewey-Vogt; Stephanie Forrest; Westley Weimer
access_depth: primary paper abstract and institutional metadata
contribution: Evaluates GenProg at larger scale with explicit compute-cost accounting.
key_findings: Reports repairs for 55 of 105 benchmark defects under the study's validation procedure.
importance: An influential scale-and-cost study whose later reanalysis illustrates evolving evaluation standards.
relevance: The manuscript can learn from the distinction between a reported test-adequate repair and independently established correctness.
transferable_idea: Report cost per independently validated retained fix, including unsuccessful and invalidated episodes.
limitations: The headline is the original study's claim, not endorsement of all patches; later plausibility audits dispute portions of this evidence.

title: SemFix: Program Repair via Semantic Analysis
authors: Hoang Duong Thien Nguyen; Dawei Qi; Abhik Roychoudhury; Satish Chandra
access_depth: primary institutional abstract and metadata
contribution: Formulates repair as constraints solved with symbolic execution and program synthesis.
key_findings: Outperforms its genetic-programming comparator on the studied subjects in repair success and speed.
importance: Shows how feedback can express semantic requirements rather than merely a verdict.
relevance: The finite contradiction certificates could become structured constraints that an agent can inspect and challenge.
transferable_idea: Compare Boolean feedback, concrete counterexamples, and independently checkable constraint evidence at matched information budgets.
limitations: Semantic synthesis is still relative to supplied tests and repair expressions; it does not establish unrestricted impossibility.

title: An Analysis of Patch Plausibility and Correctness for Generate-and-Validate Patch Generation Systems
authors: Zichao Qi; Fan Long; Sara Achour; Martin Rinard
access_depth: full text: introduction, plausibility audit, weak-proxy analysis
contribution: Audits generated patches and introduces Kali, which repairs by deleting functionality.
key_findings: Finds validation-infrastructure errors and many patches that pass weak proxies while eliminating desired behavior.
importance: A direct precedent for evaluator audits changing the interpretation of apparent repair success.
relevance: The current hidden-veto audit is not the first repair-harness validity critique.
transferable_idea: Include deletion, reject-all, and no-change controls; test acceptance logic separately from property tests.
limitations: Historical systems and datasets differ; the paper does not test LLM responses to randomized false feedback. Infrastructure must be audited too.

title: Is the Cure Worse Than the Disease? Overfitting in Automated Program Repair
authors: Edward K. Smith; Earl T. Barr; Claire Le Goues; Yuriy Brun
access_depth: full text: abstract, introduction, evaluation framing
contribution: Separates tests used to construct repairs from independent tests used to assess them.
key_findings: Across its studied bugs, passing repair tests often fails to improve held-out behavior; starting quality matters.
importance: Establishes repair overfitting as a fundamental evaluation concern predating LLMs.
relevance: The local weak-check versus bounded-property discrepancy is another manifestation of this general issue.
transferable_idea: Measure both newly corrected and newly broken cases after every revision, including initially strong candidates.
limitations: Its student-program setting does not quantify modern repository agents or deliberate false-feedback interventions.

title: Identifying Test-Suite-Overfitted Patches through Test Case Generation
authors: Qi Xin; Steven P. Reiss
access_depth: primary paper abstract and method introduction
contribution: Introduces DiffTGen, generating inputs that expose semantic differences between original and patched programs.
key_findings: Identifies 39 of 79 likely incorrect patches in its evaluation, producing distinguishing tests.
importance: Makes patch disagreement actionable through concrete tests instead of a second unexplained label.
relevance: A second-opinion tool in the manuscript should return discriminating evidence, not merely another PASS or FAIL.
transferable_idea: Generate minimal counterexamples to distinguish property-preserving edits from regressions and offer these as an intervention arm.
limitations: Correct expected outputs still require an oracle; the technique cannot eliminate specification ambiguity.

title: Investigating Test Overfitting on SWE-bench
authors: Toufique Ahmed; Jatin Ganhotra; Avraham Shinnar; Martin Hirzel
access_depth: full text: research questions, refinement protocol, methods
contribution: Studies repository-level refinement using generated tests and an LLM critic.
key_findings: Finds test overfitting and tradeoffs in mitigation; even refinement using revealed gold tests can break other behavior.
importance: A close modern precedent for the claim that additional repair steps can make working code worse.
relevance: Requires a truthful-feedback continuation control before attributing regression to a false verdict.
transferable_idea: Cross feedback truth with continuation opportunity, then evaluate original, target, and held-out behavior separately.
limitations: Its code-and-test refinement pipeline differs from a single verdict change at a verified security onset.

title: Defects4J: A Database of Existing Faults to Enable Controlled Testing Studies for Java Programs
authors: René Just; Darioush Jalali; Michael D. Ernst
access_depth: primary paper abstract and metadata
contribution: Provides reproducible real Java defects with executable tests and version-control context.
key_findings: The original release contains 357 faults from five projects.
importance: Established reusable real-bug infrastructure for controlled software-testing and repair research.
relevance: Highlights the external-validity limitation of authored finite tasks and the value of reproducible project-level instances.
transferable_idea: Separate a tightly controlled finite mechanism study from an independently sampled real-project validation tier.
limitations: Defect datasets have selection and historical-contamination risks; their presence does not certify every test oracle. Maintain reproducible versions and explicit inclusion rules.

title: The ManyBugs and IntroClass Benchmarks for Automated Repair of C Programs
authors: Claire Le Goues; Neal Holtschulte; Edward K. Smith; Yuriy Brun; Premkumar Devanbu; Stephanie Forrest; Westley Weimer
access_depth: primary project page and paper abstract
contribution: Defines repair benchmarks with reproducible defects, test suites, and categorized study objects.
key_findings: Presents 1,183 defects across fifteen C programs in two complementary datasets.
importance: Shows that benchmark construction must support specific experimental questions rather than maximize raw task count.
relevance: The manuscript's twenty named families need semantic and mechanism independence, not merely distinct labels.
transferable_idea: Publish task provenance, admissible repair space, oracle assumptions, and category-level coverage for each family.
limitations: Benchmark authors later clarify construction and harness issues; reproducibility and correctness are separate properties.

title: Automatic Patch Generation by Learning Correct Code
authors: Fan Long; Martin Rinard
access_depth: primary author research page and abstract
contribution: Introduces Prophet, ranking candidate repairs using properties learned from human patches.
key_findings: Generates correct patches for eighteen of 69 evaluated defects, with fifteen ranked first.
importance: Recognizes that many test-passing candidates compete with a much smaller set of correct repairs.
relevance: The manuscript should track selection and preservation of good candidates rather than only whether any candidate passes.
transferable_idea: Add a best-verified-candidate memory baseline and compare final output with the best candidate encountered.
limitations: Learned patch priors are fallible and benchmark-dependent; resemblance to human code does not prove security.

title: Staged Program Repair with Condition Synthesis
authors: Fan Long; Martin Rinard
access_depth: primary full-text excerpts: abstract, synthesis method, experimental framing
contribution: Combines transformation schemas, target-value search, and condition synthesis to search repairs efficiently.
key_findings: Finds more correct repairs than its compared systems on the selected benchmark.
importance: Illustrates why repair search-space design changes both candidate quality and computational cost.
relevance: Finite-mode agent experiments restrict the search space so strongly that observed behavior may reflect mode geometry.
transferable_idea: Vary candidate-language expressiveness while preserving the same semantic task and feedback intervention.
limitations: Success within a restricted repair language does not imply success for arbitrary programs or task families.

title: DirectFix: Looking for Simple Program Repairs
authors: Sergey Mechtaev; Jooyong Yi; Abhik Roychoudhury
access_depth: primary paper abstract and author publication metadata
contribution: Uses partial MaxSAT and synthesis to seek small repairs while preserving program structure.
key_findings: Integrates localization and repair to avoid explicitly enumerating every location-candidate combination.
importance: Treats minimal change as a principled repair objective.
relevance: The manuscript's AST and API changes cannot alone show useful adaptation; large changes can destroy valid behavior.
transferable_idea: Use edit size as a secondary descriptor alongside independently measured preservation and correction.
limitations: Small patches can still be wrong; structure preservation is an optimization criterion rather than a semantic guarantee. Preservation needs independent measurement.

title: Angelix: Scalable Multiline Program Patch Synthesis via Symbolic Analysis
authors: Sergey Mechtaev; Jooyong Yi; Abhik Roychoudhury
access_depth: primary institutional abstract and paper method excerpts
contribution: Uses symbolic analysis and compact repair constraints to synthesize coordinated multiline fixes.
key_findings: Repairs real software including multi-location defects and reports experience with Heartbleed.
importance: Shows a concrete route from bounded semantic constraints to more realistic repair synthesis.
relevance: The finite-policy benchmark can supply strong internal validity but must not be mistaken for full code repair.
transferable_idea: Add a semantics-based comparator on supported tasks and report which dependency structures it can repair.
limitations: Solver and repair-space restrictions remain; constraint satisfaction is only as sound as the encoded specification.

title: Getafix: Learning to Fix Bugs Automatically
authors: Johannes Bader; Andrew Scott; Michael Pradel; Satish Chandra
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 3(OOPSLA)
access_depth: primary abstract; author-hosted final publication metadata
contribution: Learns hierarchical fix patterns and ranks context-appropriate suggestions from prior human changes.
key_findings: Evaluates 1,268 fixes across six Java bug categories and reports industrial deployment.
importance: Demonstrates that realistic repair systems rely on constrained categories and contextual ranking.
relevance: The paper's general statements about coding agents should acknowledge narrower, successful repair deployments.
transferable_idea: Stratify results by mechanism and compare a learned-pattern or template baseline where applicable.
limitations: Exact-match fixes and deployment experience do not establish broad vulnerability repair or resilience to misleading checkers. Pattern specificity must be reported.

title: SapFix: Automated End-to-End Repair at Scale
authors: Alexandru Marginean; Johannes Bader; Satish Chandra; Mark Harman; Yue Jia; Ke Mao; Alexander Mols; Andrew Scott
venue: IEEE/ACM ICSE Software Engineering in Practice
access_depth: primary institutional abstract and paper introduction
contribution: Integrates test generation, fault localization, candidate repair, retesting, and developer review in production.
key_findings: Reports deployment across six large Facebook systems.
importance: Shows that the repair lifecycle and validation interface matter as much as candidate generation.
relevance: The manuscript's stop handshake and logging defects are system-level causes, not necessarily model-level failures.
transferable_idea: Separate model decisions, adapter transitions, validation, and final commitment in both logs and analysis.
limitations: Industrial null-dereference repair is a constrained setting; its operational results are not comparable to synthetic security episodes. Log provenance alongside every verdict.

title: Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
authors: Hammond Pearce; Baleegh Ahmad; Benjamin Tan; Brendan Dolan-Gavitt; Ramesh Karri
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
access_depth: primary abstract and official conference metadata
contribution: Systematically evaluates security weaknesses in Copilot-generated code under varied scenarios and prompts.
key_findings: Finds vulnerable suggestions in security-relevant generation tasks.
importance: An influential empirical basis for treating functional generation success and security separately.
relevance: Motivates the manuscript's domain but does not validate its narrow cryptographic and web checks.
transferable_idea: Include realistic vulnerability classes, prompt sensitivity, and security-specific adjudication rather than a single success label.
limitations: Early-model controlled scenarios do not estimate current deployed-agent risk or effects of iterative feedback. Replication should fix model versions and prompts.

title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
authors: Neil Perry; Megha Srivastava; Deepak Kumar; Dan Boneh
access_depth: primary paper introduction and abstract
contribution: Studies how people use an AI assistant on security-related programming tasks.
key_findings: Finds security and confidence problems in its assisted group, with meaningful differences in prompting behavior.
importance: Shows that reliance and confidence can diverge from code quality.
relevance: An adjacent human precedent for asking whether authoritative machine feedback is followed appropriately.
transferable_idea: If a later human comparison is feasible, measure evidence checking and confidence calibration separately from repair success.
limitations: Human-assistant interactions are not autonomous-agent behavior; its model, participants, and tasks limit transfer. Generalization requires new evidence.

title: Lost at C: A User Study on the Security Implications of Large Language Model Code Assistants
authors: Gustavo Sandoval; Hammond Pearce; Teo Nys; Ramesh Karri; Siddharth Garg; Brendan Dolan-Gavitt
access_depth: primary abstract and official proceedings metadata
contribution: Evaluates AI assistance in a controlled low-level C programming study with 58 participants.
key_findings: Reports a small security impact in its particular pointer-and-array task setting.
importance: Provides counterevidence to universal claims that AI assistance necessarily worsens security.
relevance: The manuscript should expect task-dependent feedback effects rather than assume a uniform harmful response.
transferable_idea: Prespecify task mechanisms that could moderate effects and report informative null or reverse effects.
limitations: This student-programmer study does not establish safety of autonomous repair or general equivalence across security domains. Mechanisms need direct tests.

title: Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models
authors: Hammond Pearce; Benjamin Tan; Baleegh Ahmad; Ramesh Karri; Brendan Dolan-Gavitt
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
access_depth: full text: methods, real-world results, reliability discussion
contribution: Evaluates prompt-based vulnerability repair across synthetic, handcrafted, and historical real-world scenarios.
key_findings: Simple scenarios are more tractable; real-world patches can pass functional and security tests while remaining implausible.
importance: Directly distinguishes test adequacy from genuine vulnerability repair in early LLM work.
relevance: Weak finite checks are a known limitation, so the new paper needs a behavioral mechanism beyond identifying them.
transferable_idea: Retain a simple-to-realistic task progression and independently inspect seemingly successful fixes.
limitations: Results concern older models and selected vulnerabilities; success on a triggering input cannot prove vulnerability removal.

title: VulRepair: A T5-Based Automated Software Vulnerability Repair
authors: Michael Fu; Chakkrit Tantithamthavorn; Trung Le; Van Nguyen; Dinh Phung
access_depth: primary institutional abstract and paper introduction
contribution: Uses a pretrained T5 architecture and subword tokenization for vulnerability patch prediction.
key_findings: Reports stronger perfect-prediction performance than its neural repair baselines.
importance: A major specialized neural repair baseline preceding conversational agents.
relevance: Its reference-match metric illustrates why syntactic similarity and security outcomes must be distinguished.
transferable_idea: Use reference similarity only as an auxiliary measure; evaluate multiple semantically valid repairs with executable properties.
limitations: Exact prediction of a developer patch is not the only correct repair, and mismatch does not establish insecurity. Separate behavioral adequacy from textual similarity.

title: Neural Transfer Learning for Repairing Security Vulnerabilities in C Code
authors: Zimin Chen; Steve Kommrusch; Martin Monperrus
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 49(1); online 2022
access_depth: primary abstract and journal reference
contribution: Introduces VRepair, transferring knowledge from general bug fixes to scarce vulnerability-fix data.
key_findings: Transfer improves repair predictions relative to training only on the small vulnerability corpus.
importance: Connects general software repair with specialized security repair.
relevance: The manuscript can test whether general repair competence predicts preservation after conflicting feedback.
transferable_idea: Separate initial repair capability from conditional post-fix behavior; compare models only on shared eligible onsets.
limitations: Prediction-based evaluation and restricted C functions do not measure agent stopping or susceptibility to false verdicts. Avoid treating model lineage as mechanism.

title: CryptoGuard: High Precision Detection of Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Massive-sized Java Projects
authors: Sazzadur Rahaman; Ya Xiao; Sharmin Afrose; Fahad Shaon; Ke Tian; Miles Frantz; Murat Kantarcioglu; Danfeng (Daphne) Yao
access_depth: primary paper abstract, introduction and author metadata
contribution: Refines program slicing to reduce false alerts in cryptographic misuse detection.
key_findings: Reports high manually checked precision on large Apache projects and substantial false-alert reductions.
importance: Demonstrates the practical importance of detector specificity and context.
relevance: A wrong FAIL should be grounded in plausible checker failure modes, not only an arbitrary hidden veto.
transferable_idea: Construct realistic false-positive interventions involving irrelevant constants, data flow, or unsupported context.
limitations: Java misuse detectors cover specific patterns; no-finding results cannot establish global cryptographic security. Specification gaps need separate treatment.

title: CrySL: An Extensible Approach to Validating the Correct Usage of Cryptographic APIs
authors: Stefan Krüger; Johannes Späth; Karim Ali; Eric Bodden; Mira Mezini
access_depth: primary proceedings abstract and paper excerpts
contribution: Defines a specification language for correct cryptographic API usage and supports automated checking.
key_findings: Encodes expert requirements that go beyond whether an API name appears in source.
importance: Supplies a principled alternative to treating API inventory changes as security-strategy changes.
relevance: The manuscript's salt, nonce, and randomness tasks require semantic usage constraints rather than name-based labels.
transferable_idea: Build task contracts from explicit usage rules and annotate which rule each revision preserves or violates.
limitations: Correct API usage is only part of security; completeness depends on the rules and analysis assumptions.

title: A Case Study of LLM for Automated Vulnerability Repair: Assessing Impact of Reasoning and Patch Validation Feedback
authors: Ummay Kulsum; Haotian Zhu; Bowen Xu; Marcelo d'Amorim
access_depth: full text excerpts: workflow, comparisons, ablations
contribution: Introduces VRpilot, iterating vulnerability-repair prompts using reasoning and external validation feedback.
key_findings: Reports improved correct-patch production and component ablations supporting feedback's utility.
importance: Direct evidence that feedback can help, counterbalancing a narrative focused solely on harm.
relevance: The strongest new contribution should explain when to follow feedback and when to verify it.
transferable_idea: Include truthful diagnostic feedback and useful counterexamples as positive controls alongside false verdicts.
limitations: Its ablations do not isolate verdict truth at a shared verified candidate; the local effect cannot be inferred from its rates.

title: IRIS: LLM-Assisted Static Analysis for Detecting Security Vulnerabilities
authors: Ziyang Li; Saikat Dutta; Mayur Naik
access_depth: primary proceedings abstract and metadata
contribution: Combines LLM-inferred taint specifications and contextual reasoning with static analysis.
key_findings: On its 120-case Java dataset, detects more vulnerabilities than baseline CodeQL while improving false-discovery performance.
importance: Shows that tool outputs depend on inferred specifications and context, not only analyzer implementation.
relevance: A second checker may share model-generated assumptions with the agent and therefore fail independently only in appearance.
transferable_idea: Record checker provenance and compare independent expert rules against model-inferred rules.
limitations: The method targets detection rather than repair; contextual inference remains fallible and dataset-specific.

title: Security Weaknesses of Copilot-Generated Code in GitHub Projects: An Empirical Study
authors: Yujia Fu; Peng Liang; Amjed Tahir; Zengyang Li; Mojtaba Shahin; Jiaxin Yu; Jinfu Chen
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology 34(8)
access_depth: full text excerpts: sampling, detector combination, results
contribution: Analyzes AI-generated snippets found in public projects and tests warning-guided repair.
key_findings: Finds security weaknesses across many CWEs; feedback repairs some but not all flagged issues.
importance: Extends controlled generation studies toward naturally occurring code.
relevance: The manuscript's Bandit reanalysis must retain the distinction between scanner findings and actual vulnerability truth.
transferable_idea: Combine complementary detectors with manual adjudication and report each tool's coverage and disagreement.
limitations: Publicly attributed snippets are selected, and static-analysis weaknesses are not equivalent to independently confirmed exploits. Detector agreement still needs independent adjudication.

title: Logs In, Patches Out: Automated Vulnerability Repair via Tree-of-Thought LLM Analysis
authors: Youngjoon Kim; Sunguk Shin; Hyoungshick Kim; Jiwon Yoon
access_depth: primary proceedings abstract and metadata
contribution: Introduces SAN2PATCH, decomposing sanitizer-guided repair into comprehension, localization, strategy, and patching.
key_findings: Reports strong repair results on VulnLoc and a newly curated vulnerability set.
importance: Provides a concrete contemporary feedback-driven vulnerability-repair architecture.
relevance: The proposed study can test which phase is redirected by misleading feedback rather than only counting edits.
transferable_idea: Instrument diagnosis, evidence gathering, patch proposal, and commitment as observable actions without claiming hidden reasoning.
limitations: Its headline repair rates depend on validation; PVBench subsequently evaluates SAN2PATCH under stronger tests. Richer reasoning cannot substitute for validation.

title: Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer
authors: Richard A. DeMillo; Richard J. Lipton; Frederick G. Sayward
access_depth: primary paper introduction and institutional metadata
contribution: Motivates mutation-based testing through small program changes and the coupling of simple and complex faults.
key_findings: Argues that exposing simple errors can provide leverage against more complex errors.
importance: A foundational rationale for testing the test suite itself.
relevance: The manuscript's authored insecure mutations are calibration challenges, not samples of model-generated failures.
transferable_idea: Create prespecified mutant classes for unsafe acceptance and false denial, and measure which oracles detect each.
limitations: Mutation adequacy is conditional on chosen operators; equivalent mutants and unrealistic fault distributions limit interpretation.

title: Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults in Software Testing?
authors: René Just; Darioush Jalali; Laura Inozemtseva; Michael D. Ernst; Reid Holmes; Gordon Fraser
access_depth: primary author abstract and metadata
contribution: Tests whether mutation detection tracks real-fault detection after controlling for coverage.
key_findings: Finds a statistically significant relationship on 357 faults in five applications, while identifying limitations.
importance: Offers empirical support for mutation calibration without treating it as infallible.
relevance: The manuscript can justify held-out mutation challenges but must avoid interpreting authored failures as population prevalence.
transferable_idea: Validate mutation classes against historical real security defects and report missed real-fault mechanisms.
limitations: The evidence comes from its studied programs; correlation does not guarantee every security mutant represents realistic agent errors.

title: Assessing Oracle Quality with Checked Coverage
authors: David Schuler; Andreas Zeller
access_depth: primary paper abstract and method introduction
contribution: Measures statements whose effects actually reach assertions rather than merely executed statements.
key_findings: Experiments indicate checked coverage can reveal weak or missing test oracles.
importance: Exposes why running code is not equivalent to checking its relevant behavior.
relevance: The historical evaluator's assertions and exception handling deserve direct scrutiny before agent outcomes are interpreted.
transferable_idea: Audit whether each security-relevant computation influences a meaningful assertion and seed assertion-breaking controls.
limitations: A computation can reach an assertion whose expected value is wrong; checked coverage does not establish specification validity.

title: Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness
authors: Laura Inozemtseva; Reid Holmes
access_depth: primary paper abstract and methods framing
contribution: Separates test-suite size from coverage when evaluating fault-detection effectiveness.
key_findings: Finds only low-to-moderate association after controlling test count; stronger coverage forms do not solve the problem.
importance: A warning against convenient proxy metrics becoming scientific targets.
relevance: The manuscript should not replace its weak checks with a high coverage percentage and call the oracle validated.
transferable_idea: Calibrate against independently specified fault classes and report detection performance in addition to structural coverage.
limitations: Mutation-based effectiveness and the chosen Java systems bound the study; coverage remains useful for finding untested regions.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Flaky Tests
authors: Qingzhou Luo; Farah Hariri; Lamyaa Eloussi; Darko Marinov
access_depth: primary paper abstract, introduction and institutional metadata
contribution: Studies nondeterministic tests and categorizes their causes and repair practices.
key_findings: Examines 201 likely flaky-test fixes across 51 open-source projects.
importance: Demonstrates a naturally occurring source of contradictory feedback for unchanged code.
relevance: A fixed hidden veto is only one failure mechanism and may produce unrealistic agent expectations.
transferable_idea: Add a separately preregistered intermittent-failure condition with repeat-check actions and honest uncertainty metadata.
limitations: Repeated execution may detect flakiness but cannot automatically determine intended behavior; retries can also hide real bugs. Report retry policy and unresolved outcomes separately.

title: Evaluating Fuzz Testing
authors: George Klees; Andrew Ruef; Benji Cooper; Shiyi Wei; Michael Hicks
access_depth: primary paper abstract and evaluation framing
contribution: Audits fuzzing evaluations and experimentally demonstrates how design choices distort comparisons.
key_findings: Finds methodological problems across 32 reviewed evaluations and shows they can change conclusions.
importance: A strong precedent for turning a local audit into generalizable experimental methodology.
relevance: The manuscript needs multiple independent subjects and repeated runs, not more nested actions mistaken for replication.
transferable_idea: Freeze budgets and targets, retain failures, and report variation and task-level outcomes before aggregate rankings.
limitations: Fuzzers differ from LLM agents; the transferable contribution is evaluation design, not a directly applicable effect size.

title: BenchChecker: Assessing the Credibility of Bug-Fixing Benchmarks for LLMs
authors: Di Wu; Xu He; Shu Wang; Kun Sun
access_depth: primary proceedings abstract and metadata
contribution: Detects likely benchmark contamination through repository-presence and patch-presence probes.
key_findings: Finds that filtering contaminated samples changes reported resolution rates on examined benchmarks.
importance: Adds training-data contamination to the validity threats facing real-repository extensions.
relevance: A matched feedback fork controls the candidate, but it does not establish that initial repair reflected fresh problem solving.
transferable_idea: Record contamination indicators and include recently constructed, semantics-validated variants as sensitivity tests.
limitations: Detection is probabilistic; removal of flagged samples can alter task difficulty and should not be treated as random filtering.

title: PATCHAGENT: A Practical Program Repair Agent Mimicking Human Expertise
authors: Zheng Yu; Ziyi Guo; Yuhang Wu; Jiahao Yu; Meng Xu; Dongliang Mu; Yan Chen; Xinyu Xing
access_depth: primary proceedings abstract and metadata
contribution: Integrates fault localization, patch generation, verification, and interaction optimization in an autonomous repair agent.
key_findings: Reports high repair success on 178 real-world vulnerabilities under its evaluation.
importance: A realistic multi-tool comparator for a prospective feedback-integrity study.
relevance: Moves the research beyond a small local model and finite mode choices toward practical repair workflows.
transferable_idea: Replicate matched feedback interventions inside a real agent with preserved source, verifier, and action records.
limitations: Its success claims are evaluator-dependent; later stronger validation studies motivate independent checking rather than reusing headline rates.

title: HACL*: A Verified Modern Cryptographic Library
authors: Jean-Karim Zinzindohoué; Karthikeyan Bhargavan; Jonathan Protzenko; Benjamin Beurdouche
access_depth: primary paper excerpts: guarantees, limitations and conclusion
contribution: Develops verified cryptographic implementations with explicit functional, memory-safety, and secret-independence guarantees.
key_findings: Shows that strong implementation guarantees can coexist with practical performance.
importance: A benchmark for precise language about what security evidence establishes.
relevance: The manuscript's bounded oracle should state its guarantees as explicitly, without calling finite example passes secure code.
transferable_idea: Use verified reference implementations where appropriate and distinguish specification, implementation, compiler, and environment assumptions.
limitations: Formal guarantees depend on the specification and trusted toolchain; they do not automatically certify every application using the library.

title: Metamorphic Testing: A Review of Challenges and Opportunities
authors: Tsong Yueh Chen; Fei-Ching Kuo; Huai Liu; Pak-Lok Poon; Dave Towey; T. H. Tse; Zhi Quan Zhou
access_depth: primary institutional abstract and accepted manuscript
contribution: Organizes testing through relations among multiple inputs and outputs when individual expected outputs are difficult to obtain.
key_findings: Identifies relation discovery, generation, and validation challenges.
importance: Provides a framework for expanding tests without pretending to possess a complete oracle.
relevance: Nonce, request authorization, and representation changes have useful relational properties beyond single examples.
transferable_idea: Prespecify valid transformations, such as irrelevant-field changes that should preserve authorization, and test checker consistency.
limitations: Incorrect metamorphic relations create false failures; independent semantic review is essential before use as feedback.

title: Using Frankencerts for Automated Adversarial Testing of Certificate Validation in SSL/TLS Implementations
authors: Chad Brubaker; Suman Jana; Baishakhi Ray; Sarfraz Khurshid; Vitaly Shmatikov
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
access_depth: primary paper abstract and introduction
contribution: Combines mutated certificates with differential testing of certificate-validation implementations.
key_findings: Finds discrepancies and security problems in complex validation logic.
importance: A concrete security example where implementations disagree despite nominally implementing the same standard.
relevance: Directly relevant to a TLS-family extension and to studying whether agents resolve conflicting checker evidence.
transferable_idea: Use independently adjudicated disagreement cases, preserving accepted-valid and rejected-invalid behaviors separately.
limitations: Disagreement is a discovery signal rather than ground truth; standards ambiguity and shared implementation errors require review. Include legitimate certificates to detect overly restrictive validation.

title: Estimating causal effects of treatments in randomized and nonrandomized studies
authors: Donald B. Rubin
access_depth: Abstract and bibliographic metadata inspected; no full-text claim
contribution: Clarifies how experimental assignment and carefully controlled observational comparisons support treatment-effect estimation.
key_findings: Randomization is preferred when feasible; observational adjustment requires explicit conditions rather than treating association as intervention.
importance: Supplies the causal vocabulary needed to turn a checker audit into a verdict-intervention experiment.
relevance: Historical R/U trajectories differ beyond their terminal verdict; exact-source equality alone does not make them randomized counterfactuals.
transferable_idea: Freeze candidate and history, randomize the delivered verdict at onset, and define potential outcomes separately for unsafe acceptance and legitimate-request denial.
limitations: Theory does not retrospectively repair missing receipts or justify generalization from five chosen families.

title: Statistics and Causal Inference
authors: Paul W. Holland
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 81(396):945–960
access_depth: Primary full-text introduction and potential-outcome sections inspected
contribution: Formalizes causal effects through potential outcomes and distinguishes causal questions from associational descriptions.
key_findings: Individual counterfactual contrasts require assumptions; randomized assignment supports population-average contrasts under a defined design.
importance: Separates three issues often conflated in the draft: identification, statistical precision, and population transport.
relevance: A selected secure onset can support a controlled within-onset comparison even though it represents no broad task population.
transferable_idea: State which state is cloned, which random inputs are coupled, and whether the target is a finite scheduled-cohort effect or a superpopulation effect.
limitations: Cloning software does not eliminate model-runtime drift, interference, or the need to define the unit.

title: The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects
authors: Paul R. Rosenbaum; Donald B. Rubin
access_depth: Abstract and bibliographic metadata inspected; no full-text claim
